t10.pacing:
*When:* Every timed set, and the real exam. The clock decides how many questions you get to attempt.

*Why:* Each question is worth the same, but not each costs the same. Time sunk into one hard question is taken from several easy ones.

*Move:*
$$t_q=\frac{T_{\rm total}}{N}$$
Here $T_{\rm total}$ is the test time and $N$ the number of questions. Set checkpoints at fixed fractions of the test. Skip anything you have not started within about 30 seconds, flag it, and return if time is left. ETS reports percent correct for tests since September 2023, so a wrong answer costs nothing. Confirm in the current bulletin, then never leave a blank.

*Example:* A test of $N=70$ questions in $120$ min.
$$t_q=\frac{120}{70}\approx1.7\ \mathrm{min},\qquad \text{checkpoint: question }35\text{ by minute }60$$
If you reach minute 60 at question 28, speed up and skip more.

*Trap:* Sinking five minutes into one derivation because you are close to the answer.

*Check:* At each checkpoint, your question number divided by $N$ should match the fraction of time used.
t10.elimination:
*When:* Answer options differ in sign, power, units or form, and you can discard some without solving.

*Why:* A wrong option often fails a test that costs seconds. Fewer survivors means less computing and a better guess if you run out of time.

*Move:*
$$\text{units}\ \to\ \text{sign}\ \to\ \text{limiting value}\ \to\ \text{symmetry}\ \to\ \text{compute}$$
Test each option against these in order and cross out failures. Compute only when two or more survive. Keep a failed option only if you are unsure about the test itself.

*Example:* How long does a ball dropped from height $h$ take to fall? The options are $\sqrt{2h/g}$, $\sqrt{2g/h}$, $2hg$ and $\sqrt{2hg}$.
$$[\sqrt{2h/g}]=\sqrt{\mathrm m\,/\,(\mathrm m/\mathrm s^2)}=\mathrm s$$
The others have units of $1/\mathrm s$, $\mathrm m^2/\mathrm s^2$ and $\mathrm m/\mathrm s$, so the first stands alone.

*Trap:* Eliminating the correct option because of one mistaken limit.

*Check:* The survivor must also behave sensibly: a larger $h$ should give a longer time.
t10.dim-limits:
*When:* The answer is a formula in several parameters, and you want to check it quickly.

*Why:* A correct formula has the right units and gives the known answer in simple special cases. A wrong one usually fails one of these.

*Move:*
$$[\text{answer}]=[\text{quantity asked}],\qquad f(\text{parameter}\to0\ \text{or}\ \infty)=\text{known result}$$
Check units first. Then set one parameter to zero, to infinity, or to a symmetric value where the physics is obvious, and see whether the formula agrees. Do this for each option and discard those that fail.

*Example:* An Atwood machine with masses $m_1$ and $m_2$. Compare two options for the acceleration.
$$a=\frac{(m_1-m_2)g}{m_1+m_2}\quad\text{versus}\quad a=\frac{(m_1+m_2)g}{m_1-m_2}$$
At $m_1=m_2$ the first gives $0$, as it should. The second diverges. With $m_2\to0$ the first gives $g$, free fall.

*Trap:* A formula can pass dimensions and still be wrong by a pure number such as a factor of 2.

*Check:* After the limits agree, check the numerical factor in one case you can solve outright.
t10.order-magnitude:
*When:* The answer options are spread by factors of ten or more, so only the power of ten matters.

*Why:* Exact arithmetic is slow and wasted when options are far apart. Rounding to one figure keeps the power of ten right, which is all you need.

*Move:*
$$x\approx a\times10^{p},\qquad \text{round each constant to one figure, add exponents, then compare}$$
Write every quantity as one digit times a power of ten. Combine the digits first, then the exponents. Choose the nearest option. If two options are close, keep a second figure.

*Example:* How many carbon atoms are in $1$ g of carbon, using $N_A\approx6\times10^{23}$ and molar mass $12$ g/mol?
$$N\approx\frac{1}{12}\times6\times10^{23}=\frac{6}{12}\times10^{23}=5\times10^{22}$$
Pick the option nearest $5\times10^{22}$.

*Trap:* Rounding errors compound over many factors. Keep one extra figure when options are within a factor of three.

*Check:* The exponent should match a rough sense of scale, such as the size of the object.
t10.full-practice:
*When:* After the main tiers are placed, and before the exam. A full set shows what drills hide: stamina, pacing and which topics fail under pressure.

*Why:* Practice only helps if mistakes become a plan. An error log turns each miss into a technique to review.

*Move:*
$$\text{set under real clock}\ \to\ \text{tag each miss}\ \to\ \text{review log}\ \to\ \text{drill weakest}\ \to\ \text{retry misses}$$
Sit the full set with no breaks beyond the real ones. After it, tag every miss with a technique id. Count misses per id. Review the ids with the most misses before the next set. Retry the missed items a week later without notes.

*Example:* A set leaves three misses.
$$\text{entropy}\times2,\quad \text{Maxwell relations}\times1$$
The entropy card and a block of entropy drills come first. The Maxwell miss is noted and checked again after the next set.

*Trap:* Reading solutions without retrying the missed items later.

*Check:* The next set should show fewer misses on the ids you reviewed.
